analysis.one_liner: Charges mining companies royalties and fees to mine gold and other hardrock minerals on federal land, and taxes production to clean up abandoned mines.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have charged mining companies royalties and fees for the first time for mining on federal land, never got a vote in the Senate.
analysis.plain_summary: Under a law from 1872, anyone can claim valuable hardrock minerals — gold, silver, copper — on federal land and mine them without paying the government anything. This bill would have changed that: miners would pay a royalty of 2 to 5 percent of the value of what they extract, annual fees to hold claims, and a fee dedicated to a fund that cleans up the hundreds of thousands of abandoned mines that leak acid and heavy metals into western streams. It would also require permits, cleanup bonds, and inspections before mining could start, and would end the practice of letting miners buy federal land outright. The bill never got a vote: it died in the Senate Energy Committee after one hearing.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and residents of western states and tribal lands, who currently pay to clean up abandoned hardrock mines that leak acid mine drainage and toxic metals into water. The bill would shift cleanup costs onto mining companies through royalties and a reclamation fee, and would require companies to post bonds covering cleanup and long-term water treatment before mining begins. It also protects public lands by requiring permits for mining that disturbs land and water.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and western communities near mines

how_it_helps.text: For the first time, hardrock miners on federal land would pay a royalty of 2-5 percent of the value of production, money that currently goes entirely to the mining company [S3].
It ends the 1872 practice of letting miners buy federal land (patenting a claim), and imposes annual maintenance and location fees on claims [S3].
It requires permits, reclamation plans, and bonds big enough to cover cleanup and long-term water treatment before mining starts, so companies cannot walk away from polluted sites [S3].
It creates a fund, financed by mining royalties and fees, to clean up abandoned mines that leak acid drainage and pollutants in western states and on Indian land [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies operating on federal land, who would pay royalties of 2-5 percent of production value, annual claim maintenance fees of $150 per claim, land-use fees, and a reclamation fee of up to 1 percent of production value, plus bonds for reclamation and long-term water treatment. Some costs could be passed to consumers of mined metals.

drawbacks.text: New royalties of 2-5 percent of production value, annual maintenance fees of $150 per claim, land-use fees, and an abandoned-mine reclamation fee of up to 1 percent of production value would raise costs for mining companies, and some marginal operations could become uneconomic, potentially affecting jobs in mining communities [S3].

The bill requires exploration and mining permits, financial assurance bonds, and quarterly inspections, which adds permitting time and paperwork for operators, including small claim holders, though it waives the maintenance fee for small holders with 10 or fewer claims [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits were real and one-sided: the public gets royalties and cleanup money for mineral wealth that is otherwise given away, and taxpayers stop absorbing reclamation costs. The costs fall on the mining industry in the form of royalties, fees, and stricter permitting, and an honest supporter would acknowledge that new royalties and permitting costs could make some marginal mines uneconomic and slow domestic production of minerals like gold, copper, and uranium. The bill's own review provision would have required the Interior Department to report on exactly that impact [S3]. The royalty cap of 5 percent was modest by international standards, so the bill was a middle course, not a shutdown of mining.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which held one hearing but never approved it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The Senate introduced the bill on April 2, 2009 and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources [S5].
The committee held a hearing on July 14, 2009, printing the testimony as S.Hrg. 111-116, but never reported the bill to the full Senate [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill received no floor vote and no House counterpart action, and it expired when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mining companies keep mining federal land without paying royalties, and taxpayers continue to shoulder abandoned-mine cleanup costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mining companies and royalty-free status quo

for.name: Jeff Bingaman
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-NM), Chair of Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and used his committee to hold a hearing on hardrock mining reform [S5].

against.name: Mining industry and western-state opponents
against.role: Hardrock mining companies and allied western interests
against.what_they_did: Opposed royalty and patent-reform legislation of this kind; the bill never advanced past a committee hearing.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee majority (no markup)
against.what_they_did: Held a hearing but never voted the bill out of committee, keeping it off the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat and its six cosponsors were all Democrats, but the opposition that kept it in committee is not documented in the record, so the partisan shape of the failure is inferred rather than shown by any vote.

industries.note: The bill would end free and near-free access to federal minerals, impose royalties and annual fees for the first time, and require costly reclamation bonds. Its defeat preserved the 1872 status quo in which miners pay no royalties for federal hardrock minerals.

industries.industry: Taxpayers and residents of western mining states
industries.note: Residents of abandoned hardrock mine states would gain a dedicated cleanup fund and stronger water-protection rules. Had the bill passed, those gains would have come from industry payments rather than taxes; because it died, cleanup continues to be paid for largely by the public.
